name: Sanchin
description: The foundation of Goju-Ryu, a kata that unites body, mind and technique.

origin.title: Origin
origin.content: Sanchin has clear roots in Southern China (Fujian). It is one of the few kata that occurs in both Okinawan Uechi-, Goju-, and Pangainoon/Kombatie styles. Originally it was called sānzhàn in Mandarin. In Okinawa, Kanryō Higaonna learned it from his Chinese master and passed it on to Miyagi. In Shuri, Sokon Matsumura also learned it in China and passed it on in Okinawa. Thus Sanchin appears in all major lines. Goju-ryu knows two variants: Miyagi's closed-fist sanchin dai ichi and Higaonna's original open-hand sanchin dai ni (later also made closed by Juhatsu Kyoda). The kata belongs to the oldest karate forms and is believed to have existed before 1800.

transmission.title: Transmission to Goju-Ryu
transmission.content: Sanchin is the first kata that Miyagi Sensei taught (except for basic exercises). Higaonna introduced the Naha-style Sanchin (with open hands) in Miyagi's training. Miyagi made his own variant with closed fists (for practical reasons). So there have been two Sanchin within Goju from the beginning. These are preserved to this day; the 'Miyagi-' and 'Higashionna-Sanchin' are both sometimes still corrected in breathing and fist work. Other styles (Isshin, Shito, Kyokushin, Wado) have also adopted Sanchin, which shows the central role of this kata.

historicalDevelopment.title: Historical Development
historicalDevelopment.content: The core of Sanchin is unchanged: heavy physical training in sanchin-dachi, with intense ibuki breathing and isometric tension. The only important historical differences are (1) closed vs open fists (like between Yamazato vs Kyoda) and (2) light stylistic accents per Dojo. Funakoshi renamed the Shuri line Sanchin to Hangetsu (半月) for Shotokan, which is essentially an electrified version. Within Goju, however, Sanchin is identical to how Higaonna knew it. Traditionally, Sanchin is considered heishugata (hanging breath), which makes a deep difference with Tensho.

technicalFeatures.title: Technical and Philosophical Characteristics
technicalFeatures.content: Sanchin is the foundation of Goju. It is performed in sanchin-dachi (triangle stance). The kata consists of very tight, repetitive movements: high defenses and strikes and gradual shifts of posture. Important is the ibuki breathing: exhaling more forcefully during each tension. The goal is to strengthen the body (muscle and bone strengthening) and the mind (perseverance). Philosophically, Sanchin revolves around internal power and concentration: it emphasizes ki development and the transition from natural to conscious breathing technique. The motto "Karate ni sente nashi" is sometimes shown in Sanchin through blocks instead of initiate. Sanchin contains hardly any open hands (exception Higaonna's version) and no kicks; it is purely upper-body and stance.

controversy.title: Controversy/Variations within Goju-Ryu
controversy.content: The main discussion concerns mainly the implementation of breathing and the fist: some Goju schools teach two Sanchin (open and closed), others only one. There are also disagreements about tempo (slow vs slightly faster). Yet all Goju-Ryu's see Sanchin as the foundation. The term "three battles" has also been quite open to interpretation in Goju (sometimes seen as connection of body/breath/mind). Outside Goju, Sanchin sometimes got a different name (Hangetsu, Sanseiru in Uechi), but within Goju it has remained stable.

relationships.title: Relationship to Other Kata/Systems
relationships.content: Sanchin is the model for other kata within Goju. It shares much with Tensho (the "Yin" counterpart). Uechi-Ryū also uses Sanchin (with open hands), and Isshin-ryū has two almost identical Sanchin (reflection of both Goju versions). In a broader sense, Sanchin connects Goju with Chinese styles such as White Crane and Pangainoon, because it uses exactly the same stance and beat as "San Zhan" in those systems. Whoever masters Sanchin has learned a universal principle that appears everywhere in traditional martial arts.

modernPractice.title: Use in Modern Practice
modernPractice.content: Sanchin is still practiced daily in most Goju-ryu dojos, often as a warm-up or as a separate strength exercise. It is the standard form for beginning brown belts. Sanchin shows hardly any competition functions (unless special Kihon-tai-ko contests), but it forms the backbone of traditional Goju training. In competitions, the principles of Sanchin (stability, breathing technique) do form the basis for interpretations in other kata. Furthermore, Sanchin is used in health aspects (trembling or exercises) because of the well-known body saying "A Sanchin per day…".

nameAndMeaning.title: Name and Meaning
nameAndMeaning.content: Sanchin (三戦) means "three battles" or "three struggles". Literally it is Japanese/Chinese for three (三, san) and battle/war (戦, chin). Traditionally this is interpreted as the struggle to unite shin-ki-tai (mind, technique, body). Other interpretations are "three parties" (technique, breath, posture). In essence, the name stands for the three aspects of strength training that Sanchin brings together.
